    <item>
      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/pet-memorial-jewelry-small-business</link>
      <description><p>A layoff and a leap of faith convinced Katie Teixeira she had what it takes to run her own business</p><p>In 2010, Katie Teixeira adopted a kitten found all alone in an abandoned house. The kitten – so tiny she fit in the palm of Teixeira’s hand – needed to be bottle-fed every few hours. For weeks, Teixeira set her alarm for middle-of-the-night feedings and drove home on her lunch break to care for the kitten she named Milo. As the cat grew, so did the connection between them.</p><p>“We just bonded,” Teixeira says. “Like mother and daughter.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/pet-memorial-jewelry-small-business">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 17 Oct 2026 21:33:04 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Retailers on Dublin’s O’Connell Street hit with legal notices under revamp plan]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/retailers-on-dublins-oconnell-steet-hit-with-legal-notices-under-revamp-plan/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/retailers-on-dublins-oconnell-steet-hit-with-legal-notices-under-revamp-plan/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000More than a dozen retailers and restaurants on Dublin’s O’Connell Street are facing legal action over unauthorised signs and shop fronts as part of a drive to revitalise the capital’s main thoroughfare.

The businesses facing enforcement cases include Circle K, Peter Mark and Allcare Pharmacy, Ned Kelly’s Casino and several Asian diners.

It follows the appointment earlier this year of high-profile civil servant Robert Watt to lead the Dublin City Development Company. This was formed to deliver on recommendations from Dublin City Taskforce, which was set up by the Government to advise on how to revitalise O’Connell Street, tackle dereliction and improve security.

Following a review of O’Connell Street premises by Watt’s new group, 13 enforcement cases have been opened by Dublin City Council against traders and building owners on the street since the beginning of September.

The cases relate to changes to shopfronts without proper permission, unauthorised neon displays, digital advertising boards, canopies and flags, which are covered by Special Planning Control Scheme (SPCS) bylaws that cover O’Connell Street.

Businesses named in the enforcement cases include Circle K, Paddywagon Tours, Peter Mark and Allcare Pharmacy, who face enforcement cases over unauthorised signage in their shop windows.

The council case records showed an enforcement case has also been opened into Ned Kelly’s Casino over digital and neon signage, a canopy and outdoor screens which the council said was non-compliant with planning conditions.

Meanwhile, Imperial Entertainment, a casino, faces an enforcement case over “intensification of signage to front facade”. A separate case for 55-56 O’Connell Street Upper, from which casino operator Carlton Entertainment Group trades, was opened over canopies and flags erected without permission.

Asian-style buffet Fortune Terrace Buffet and sushi bar Encha face enforcement proceedings over unauthorised signage in their store windows. Dublin City Council has also said that ramen and sushi restaurant Yuriko put in place its wooden shopfront without proper permission.

Other retailers that face new enforcement cases are Pick & Pay, Arisu Photo Booth and Green Island Supermarket, all over signage on their windows and facade.

Plan for O’Connell Street restaurant approved, but it is banned from serving takeaways

Further planning enforcement cases were opened earlier this year for the O’Connell Street premises occupied by Smiles Dental, which attached advertisement signs to a protected structure without permission, and Flanagans Restaurant over unauthorised signage. These cases have since been closed.

The Dublin City Development Company, led by Watt, has no power to enforce planning rules. The new body is understood to have flagged the planning breaches with Dublin City Council through its complaints procedure and following a review of the complaints, the council opened enforcement cases.

Failure to comply with the planning enforcement procedure can result in fines of up to €5,000.

Earlier this month, Watt – who has been seconded from the Civil Service to the new role – told the Irish Planning Institute’s autumn conference Dublin City Council had not imposed planning laws properly on O’Connell Street businesses.

There are two SPCS in place at present in central Dublin, which cover Grafton Street, O’Connell Street and their surrounding areas. The SPCS set out a number of policies and objectives on architectural conservation, property uses, building heights, advertising signs and shopfronts, vacancy and civic identity.

Earlier this month, the SPCS was used by Dublin City Council to bar a new restaurant being planned for Ulster Bank’s former O’Connell Street branch in Dublin from operating any takeaway food service.

Long-standing concerns have been aired by city councillors about the concentration of fast-food outlets on O’Connell Street, from which about a dozen provide takeaway services.

]]><![CDATA[Recent mergers may face investigation by regulators following Irish Government error]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Businesses that agreed mergers or takeovers in recent weeks may face investigation by competition regulators as a result of a Government mistake, it has emerged.

Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke, increased the financial values at which mergers must be notified to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in July.

However, his department has confirmed that Burke’s order lapsed on September 30th, when it emerged that the Oireachtas had not approved it on time, exposing deals agreed or completed since that date to possible investigation by the commission.

The ministerial order increased the financial threshold at which mergers must be notified to the commission to a combined turnover of €100 million or more, from €60 million.

Competition law obliges the CCPC to investigate deals meeting the threshold to ensure they do not damage competition in their relevant markets, before approving them, often with conditions meant to protect competition.

As the order lapsed on September 30th, the old rules have applied since then.

So mergers or takeovers agreed or completed since then, where the parties’ combined turnover is €60 million or more, and two of those involved have sales of at least €10 million each, may face investigation by the commission.

The CCPC is advising businesses involved in transactions either agreed or completed since September 30th to consider if they meet the old threshold and whether they should notify it of the deal.

The commission pledged not to investigate any parties to deals done in those circumstances for “gun jumping”, that is completing the transactions before getting its approval.

Any mergers completed between July 1st and September 30th were subject to the increased threshold, that is a combined turnover of €100 million or more, and at least €15 million for two of the parties involved.

According to the department, Burke’s order increasing the threshold was laid before the Oireachtas, but did not get the approval of both the Dáil and Seanad within the time set out by the Competition Act, 2002.

“As a result, the order ceased to have effect,” said a spokeswoman, who confirmed that the error emerged following a department review.

The Act requires the CCPC to investigate mergers for their likely impact on competition, but gives the Minster the power to raise the thresholds for such inquiries to keep them in line with inflation and economic circumstances.

Ministerial orders, also dubbed statutory instruments, generally need Oireachtas approval before taking effect.

Burke signed the order on June 10th, branding the move part of his efforts to cut red tape for business.

The Minister said at the time that he increased the financial notification threshold in response to a public consultation that he held earlier this year.

The CCPC favoured an increase as it allowed the regulator to focus resources on deals more likely to have a meaningful impact on competition and consumers.

The last increase was in 2019, before the significant inflation that followed Covid and the war in Ukraine.

The commission has the power to “call in” transactions below the €100 million value where it believes they could affect competition.

The department will work with the CCPC to “progress revised merger notification thresholds at the earliest opportunity in 2027,″ according to its spokeswoman. The law allows only one change each year.

]]>Orla Murray/Coalesce<![CDATA[CRH analysts play catch-up as Wall Street braces for rare earnings miss]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/17/crh-analysts-play-catch-up-as-wall-street-braces-for-rare-earnings-miss/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/17/crh-analysts-play-catch-up-as-wall-street-braces-for-rare-earnings-miss/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 12:28:38 +0000The honeymoon is over for CRH chief executive Jim Mintern.

Shares in the building materials and solutions giant jumped more than 40 per cent from the start of his tenure early last year to an all-time high of $131.55 in early January – valuing the business at almost $88 billion (€78 billion).

The rally was fuelled by Mintern’s strategy, unveiled last September, which pledged $40 billion in investment and shareholder returns over five years, alongside annual revenue growth of 7-9 per cent and higher profit margins. Anticipation of the company joining the prestigious S&P 500 index late last year also boosted sentiment, as did a consistent buyer of its shares: CRH itself.

CRH spent $1.2 billion buying back and cancelling its own stock in 2025. It brought the total spent under a repurchase programme that started under Mintern’s predecessor, Albert Manifold, in 2018 to $9.6 billion.

However, the group’s stock has slumped by 40 per cent from those January highs to a low of $78.60 on Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange, where it moved its main listing two years ago. North America accounted for more than 70 per cent of its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) last year.

Consensus analysts’ earnings forecasts have trended lower over the course of the year as the Middle East crisis has driven up fuel costs and had a knock-on impact on US house building.

CRH’s energy costs surged more than 17 per cent in the second quarter and were running at an annualised $2.33 billion. The conflict has also sent mortgage rates higher, compounding the affordability problems that were already weighing on US house building.

The average rate on a 15-year fixed-rate mortgage now exceeds 6.7 per cent, up from 5.5 per cent a year ago, according to Freddie Mac, the government-backed mortgage finance company.

With CRH due to unveil its latest quarterly results on October 29th, a number of analysts are beginning to contemplate something rare: an earnings miss from a company with a strong reputation for delivering on its guidance.

Taking a red pen in recent weeks to his forecasts for a host of US construction materials groups, Truist Securities analyst Keith Hughes now sees CRH’s Ebitda coming in at $7.87 billion. While that would mark 2.5 per cent growth on 2025, it would come in below CRH’s own forecast of a figure between $8.1 billion and $8.5 billion.

“The cut at CRH is particularly notable given a long history of hitting numbers, but we now see the possibility of an estimate range reduction,” Hughes warned.

He’s not alone. Shane Carberry of Goodbody, one of the group’s corporate brokers, recently shaved 3 per cent off his Ebitda estimate and now sees it coming in at $7.99 billion. Still, the consensus among analysts, for now, is that CRH will achieve the lower end of its guidance.

Jefferies analysts have said CRH faces “a significant effort” to reach that lower end of its full-year target as cost inflation continues apace. But, for now, they reckon that acquisitions “may bridge the gap”.

Under Manifold, CRH transformed through a series of large acquisitions – and, as importantly, divestments of unwanted assets – from being a business that essentially crushed big rocks into cement, aggregates and asphalt to become a vertically integrated leading infrastructure player in North America.

Mintern has sharpened CRH’s focus even more on what he calls three mega-trends: continuing investment in the transport system, from roads to airports; a need to develop water management; and the re-industrialisation of the US.

AI data centres are among the hottest re-industrialisation plays, with the Trump administration placing them at the heart of America’s industrial revival – betting that they will power the factories of the future and give the US a competitive edge.

Mintern said on a call with analysts in July that CRH was active on 200 data centre projects, with 85 per cent of all current construction in this area within 25 miles of one of the group’s locations.

CRH to buy aggregates operations in Denmark and Finland

The world’s largest five hyperscalers – large-scale cloud computing and technology companies, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle – are expected to spend almost $700 billion this year on US data centres, according to JP Morgan. Construction accounts for about 15 per cent of total development costs.

But while the infrastructure and non-residential construction sectors accounted for more than two-thirds of CRH’s global revenues last year, 32 per cent came from house building, repair and remodelling.

US home completions slumped almost 13 per cent in the first eight months of the year, according to US Census Bureau data. And data for September is due to be reported next Tuesday. With builders grappling with rising interest rates and weak demand, they’re unlikely to provide much relief.

An earnings miss looks more than priced in at CRH, however.

Truist’s new price target of $105 for the stock – after cutting its forecasts – points to about 25 per cent upside.

The group’s enterprise value – its market capitalisation plus net debt – stands at less than 8.8 times the bottom end of its full-year Ebitda forecast. While that is in line with its 10-year average, CRH has spent much of the last two years trading between 10 and 12 times earnings, after enjoying a valuation re-rating following the move of its primary listing to New York.*

The consensus price goal among analysts of $127 suggests more than 50 per cent.

CRH is also poised to tilt further towards infrastructure with the expected completion early next year of its $8.5 billion acquisition of Dallas-based Arcosa – the biggest of more than 1,200 deals in the group’s history.

The honeymoon may be over. But could delivery on the promises of the Arcosa deal woo Wall Street investors again?

*Updates to amend the valuation multiple reference

]]>Eddie Keogh/Imagination<![CDATA[From dereliction to Airbnb, the Gaeltacht is being destroyed by the housing crisis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000As winter looms, the evening is so pitch black on Inis Meáin that the few street lights across the sea on Inis Mór make Kilronan look like Manhattan. In the silent night, voices travel, and the low murmur of people chatting leads to the Halla Naomh Eoin, which doubles as the local community centre and the school – the beating heart of the least populated of the Aran Islands.

Inis Meáin hosts one of the country’s few all-Irish boarding schools and it is full of life, always oversubscribed with teenagers enthusiastically embracing island life and its language. Tonight’s meeting is about what will happen in a few years, when these students – both locals and outsiders – become adults, and whether they can settle on the island, rear families, continue to speak Irish and infuse the community with vibrancy.

The impediment on Inis Meáin is housing. Irish-speaking adults who want to live here have few options as prices have gone through the roof for the tiny number of homes that come on the market. Meanwhile, restrictive planning laws mean locals cannot build new homes for their children on their plots.

Ireland’s islands are an essential part of Irishness, an integral part of our heritage and culture and one of the last bastions of Irish as a living, working, breathing, everyday language.

Tonight’s meeting is organised by a group of young Gaeilgeoirí activists called Tinteán (“níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin”), whose basic message is that if young Gaeilgeoirí can’t afford to live in the Gaeltacht, it will die very soon. Ironically, we are just a few hundred yards from the cottage where JM Synge spearheaded the Gaelic Revival.

Without people, there is no revival.

According to the latest census, the country’s island population has fallen below 3,000 for the first time. To put this into context, in 1841 there were 48,000 people living on the islands off the western seaboard. Today the average age on the islands is 59 - in contrast to the rest of the country, where it is 43 – and more than one in five of the islands’ population are aged 65 years and older.

The crucial age group between 20 and 35 accounts for just 7.9 per cent of the islands’ population, as opposed to 25 per cent for the State as a whole.

Meanwhile, just 5 per cent of the islands’ population is under four years old, compared with an average of 8 per cent nationally.

These population dynamics mean only one thing: catastrophic decline and, along with a disappearing population, a disappearing language and culture. What would Synge think?

It is essential that the population decline is reversed. At a time when the Irish language has rarely been more popular, when thousands of people are learning and in some cases relearning it, the Gaeltacht itself is being destroyed by the refusal to do the very thing that generations of people from the west of Ireland did all over the world: build houses. Young families make communities, and if they have no places to live then the community dies or becomes more like a museum – visited by curious onlookers during the holiday season, but for all intents and purposes, dead.

One of the main issues is that homes have become trophy assets. When a house here comes up for sale, it is marketed online to everyone from London to New York to Mount Merrion. There is a burgeoning national and international market for property in the west of Ireland, and this process elbows out the local people, pushing prices way out of reach for the average islander.

In addition, the tourist market, so long the source of summer income, has changed dramatically.

Airbnb and Booking.com have made it so attractive for property owners to rent out their places short term that these potential homes are taken off the rental market for young Gaeilgeoirí who can’t afford to compete in trophy auctions. In many cases they are being given the option to rent until the summer comes, and then weekly rents skyrocket for the tourist season and the families must find somewhere else to live until September. They are in effect school-year residents, and that oddly nomadic existence rarely encourages people to put down roots.

Naturally, as more and more rural hotels have been turned over to refugees, tourist bed capacity falls, putting more pressure on the existing housing stock.

Life on Inis Meáin: ‘Some people will say there’s nothing here, but in fact there is everything here’

Another issue is vacancy – and ultimately dereliction, because an uninhabited house doesn’t stand a chance against Atlantic storms for long. For example, according to the local community office, on Inis Meáin there are 149 houses, of which 65 are uninhabited. Nearly half of all the homes on an island with a housing crisis stand empty.

So what can be done?

We know that people respond to incentives, positive and negative. With respect to building houses in the Gaeltacht to enable Gaeilgeoir families to live here, the key is to create the incentives to make the local housing market work. Considering the fact that there are vacant houses on the island, what might make the owners put them on the market?

At the moment, capital gains must be paid if you sell a vacant property. This is an obvious impediment to selling. Why go through the hassle of selling, particularly an old family house split between a few children, if the government gets 31 per cent of the profit? What about specifically cancelling capital gains on the islands in order to lubricate supply? Make it easy to sell. Such a move would change the conversation about selling.

A buyer’s tax break, specifically for Gaeilgeoirí, like the Temple Bar tax breaks for residents in the 1990s, would bias buying to Irish speakers.

On the planning side, what about setting a quantity of homes to be built by locals every year, based on demand and family structure, allowing the residents to solve their own problems? This would give local people the ability to build on their own island, for their own community.

‘It’s just like a match made in heaven’: Family of seven who moved to Inis Meáin urge others to follow

Even if these initiatives were embraced, there is still the issue of the cost of island life – which is far in excess of anything on the mainland. Those of us who don’t live on small islands don’t realise that the sea is a big cost driver. Think about getting material to the island, renting the truck to bring the materials to the harbour on the mainland, renting the boat to bring the stuff across, finding the workers to do the job, putting them up while they are working, and so on. All these things cost money, yet the income of Ireland’s islanders is far below the national average.

What about making island life tax-free for Gaeilgeorí, treating the people the way we treat US multinational capital? When we cut corporation tax, activity responded. The same would apply with income tax, excise duty and VAT on islands.

If we are talking about the Gaeltacht and the language, what about making living on the island tax free for Gaeilgeori? The sums of money would be tiny for a country with an annual budget of €147 billion. We are talking about only a few thousand people initially. The cost is minuscule and the prize, the preservation of a way of life and a language that has been spoken continuously in this part of the country for more than 2,500 years, is enormous.

This morning I asked a local about the weather and he responded, “Tá sé leathghlas ceart go leor,” or, “It’s a bit half grey all right.” (Down here glas isn’t green, it’s grey.) The half grey refers to the sea, the sky and heavy clouds, and the colour of the rocks, the limestone and the horizon where the sea and the clouds meet in a misty angry grey haze. This linguistic richness comes from hundreds of generations inscribing their language with colour, significance and their own meaning.

Imagine losing this for the sake of a few pennies.

]]>Jade W <![CDATA[How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Perhaps nobody in Government had heard the old sales business adage: the first one to name a price always loses.

“Say what you want,” says the first observer, “but unions are regulated, there are rules they have to observe and they do because of the potential consequences.”

Most workers – many in modestly paid jobs and feeling the pinch of rising grocery, fuel and accommodation costs – were more put out by the expiry of the last pay deal in June.

It came at a time when prices were on an upward trajectory but the Government had not indicated when they might get around to ensuring their wages were raised accordingly.

Predictably, there is now something of a blame game as to why talks on a new agreement were delayed beyond the expiry of the last deal in June. What is undisputed is that a couple of exploratory meetings in June went poorly.

This, they argue, would have left the negotiators on the employer side with no leverage at all as they sought improved productivity through changes to work practice around artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid working or anything else.

Callinan’s repeated calls this week for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to get involved are likely rooted in this, it is suggested by veterans of the pre-crash system of engagement during the “social partnership” from 1987 to 2009. Martin, they observe, is the only survivor on the Government side of how that worked and they would like to see his department reassert the control it used to exert over the negotiations.

Martin taking over might not look good for Chambers. However, Callinan made it clear on Friday that the shape of the preliminary talks process was hammed over a call with the Taoiseach.

The answer, some observers suggest, could be a short-term deal to get over the current impasse and allow everyone to come back when the tensions have eased. An alternative would be an agreement with a robust review clause for pay.

Both sides will likely agree on one thing if there is to be a short-term agreement: they will want to avoid being back in this current stalemate any sooner than they have to be.

Apple is pricey not only relative to its own history but to all but one of its magnificent seven peers (Tesla, of course). For historical reasons, 65 ended up as the widely accepted retirement age, but for a large part of human history, there was no such thing as formal retirement. People simply worked until they became incapable of doing so.

We have Bismarck to thank for introducing the concept of a modern state pension in the 19th century, with the retirement age set at 70 – at a time when few enough people lived to see that age. It was also 70 when the Old Age Pensions Act came into force in Ireland in 1908.

The qualifying age was subsequently adjusted downwards to where we are today, although a report produced in May of this year for the Financial Planning Standards Board suggests that while it’s nominally 65, many Irish people now expect to work until the age of 70 to maintain their standard of living.

Almost 80 per cent of those surveyed also felt financially unprepared for retirement, with a critical knowledge gap between what they were putting into their pension fund and how much income they thought that fund would provide when the time came.

Money, or having enough of it, pretty much tops the lists of concerns voiced by those facing retirement. This is closely followed by anxiety about filling the time previously taken up by work.

“Money is terribly important and, in an ideal world, you would start thinking about it long before you retire, maybe seven to 10 years before the planned date, because the sanest and most tax-effective way to save for retirement is by contributing to a pension scheme,” says Paul Kenny, a veteran of the pensions industry and Ireland’s first pensions ombudsman, who now leads courses for the Retirement Planning Council designed to get people retirement fit.

“Things happen that can radically change when people retire, such as illness, redundancy or an accident,” Kenny says. “Then there are those who put things on the long finger and suddenly they’re facing retirement with no financial plan.

“But all is not lost. Last-minute additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) are an option. How much you can put in is limited by your income in the final year and how much you can claim against tax, but they’re worth considering,” Kenny says.

AVCs are supplementary payments into your pension fund. If you’re in your late fifties, you can get tax relief on as much as 35 per cent of your salary if you put it into your pension fund. Above 60, that percentage jumps to 40 per cent.

So if you have just turned 60 and are earning €90,000, with normal pension contributions of 6 per cent, or €5,400, you can put up to a further €30,600 into your pension, assuming you have it. For many, it is a way of beefing up retirement income in a tax-efficient manner if they come into a windfall, such as an inheritance.

“When you’re looking at your overall money picture, an awful lot also depends on what kind of pension scheme you’re in because, in some cases, if you’re already getting the maximum from a scheme, AVCs are not going to do you any good. So, you need to know what you’re in and the benefits,” Kenny says.

“Annuities and approved retirement funds (ARFs) may also come up when discussing retirement financial planning,” Kenny adds. Both are products related to after-retirement income, not saving for retirement.

“An annuity, which will guarantee a payment for your lifetime, will be bought from an insurance company with the money in your pension fund and will very much tie you to what are currently low interest rates. Annuities are based on life expectancy and bond yields, and if interest rates are low, bond yields are low, so you’re locking yourself into a low interest rate for life.

“With ARFs, rather than lock your money into an annuity at a point in time, it remains invested after your retirement, with the retiree drawing down a certain portion of the fund each year.

“It’s crucial how you invest the money because that’s what will determine the capacity to draw down over the rest of your life. So, it’s really important to get good advice.

“ARFs are generally run by insurance companies, and they’re investing in massive numbers of different assets all over the world, something you could never do on your own, and this spreads the risk. They pay you the monies you are drawing down and take care of things like PAYE. An ARF gives you flexibility; if you really need money, you can make a drawdown and pay the necessary tax.”

Kenny says that the one thing to watch with ARF investments is the charges.

“If you’re being offered ‘hello money’ in the form of a bonus allocation, be careful. There’s only one person paying for that. So, the message is to go for the lowest charges. Anything over 1 per cent should be viewed with suspicion.”

Assuming the money side of things is under control, the next burning question for many prospective retirees is what to do with their time.

The psychosocial infrastructure is the term used to describe what a community, such as a workplace, provides to the individual. For better or for worse, this means having colleagues, work to do, and company events to attend. Losing this infrastructure can be a difficult adjustment, especially for those who have been defined by their job (often those in senior positions and the professions) or in whose life work was the dominant feature.

Kenny suggests reframing “all the time I have on my hands” to see it as a bonus, not a negative. “You’re getting back 50+ hours a week and why would you sit there and twiddle your thumbs when there is so much you could do?” he says.

“First of all, some people still want to work, so explore the options. Can you continue to work with reduced hours or part-time at your existing company with less pressure?

“Often people don’t want to keep doing what they’ve done for years, but that shouldn’t be a deterrent to doing something else. It’s really a question of looking for what’s available. If someone is prepared to work voluntarily rather than needing paid employment, then that opens another avenue.

“Sharing your talents, life and work skills with others can be invaluable and it feels good to give back. There are many charitable organisations which would bite your hand off if you had the skills to revamp an outdated system or update a website, for example.”

Retirees often get asked to join a board and, for many, it’s a good way of staying in touch. However, Kenny raises a warning flag. “Check the number of subcommittees because what looks like a once-a-month commitment can suddenly become twice a week,” he says.

Kenny adds age-appropriate exercise into the retiree timetable and also something to keep the brain agile. Both learning a new language and taking up a musical instrument for the first time are seen as particularly good ways to challenge the grey matter.

“The education and training boards offer a huge variety of hobby and other courses, with many of them heavily subsidised and run during the day. Then there are the more formal courses at Third Level for those who want to go the academic route,” Kenny says.

“Then come the hobbies which split into things you do alone and things you do with other people. I know of a gentleman who retired at 76 having known nothing but farming all his life. “The wonderful thing about any of these activities is that they bring you into contact with new people who have no idea about who you are based on what you used to do,” Kenny adds. “In a sense, you get your personal identity back, and maybe that’s still a 25-year-old trying to break loose.”

]]>Halfpoint<![CDATA[House prices: Who is getting it right, the CSO, MyHome or Daft?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000In the lead-up to the property crash of 2008 there was – let’s just say – unease about the number of estate agencies publishing what you might call self-interested house-price surveys.

Critics said their reports, and some of the commentary that went with them, were deliberately amplifying positive trends to encourage transactions.

When things began to sour, the “endless growth” narrative around Irish property gave way to the soft-landing narrative: “Okay, things have got a little frothy, there will be a modest correction, but the market is still structurally sound.”

When that thesis collapsed, and Ireland suffered the biggest peak-to-trough property crash of any country, property-price surveys (industry ones) were blamed for exacerbating the problem.

The task of producing an accurate data series on property price trends was given to the Central Statistics Office (CSO). In 2011 the agency began producing the Residential Property Price Index (RPPI), which remains the State’s official indicator of price trends.

A decade and a half later the industry barometers have crept back into the mix, led by the State’s two main property portals: MyHome and Daft. (MyHome is owned by The Irish Times Group).

While both companies’ quarterly reports are viewed as highly credible, they contain structural biases. Foremost, they base their quarterly surveys on asking prices rather than sold prices. In a sellers’ market, where buyers can get into bidding wars, these metrics can underestimate prices. The reverse is true when the market turns.

“From 2024 through to the spring of this year, transaction prices rose faster than list prices, and buyers typically paid well over the list price,” author of the Daft report Ronan Lyons said in the company’s latest survey.

Irish house prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit a price ceiling

“That has now reversed. Nationally, list prices are rising over two percentage points faster than transaction prices, the widest gap since 2023,” he said.

While Daft commands a larger market share of listings nationally, Daft and MyHome are said to be neck and neck (in terms of the listings market) in Dublin and Leinster, with most listings on both portals coming from estate agents.

Are we turning a corner on housing?

There are also quarterly surveys from Sherry Fitzgerald, Douglas Newman Good (DNG) and the Real Estate Alliance (REA), which use different methodologies.

At the moment they all tell the same story: house prices are still rising but at a slower pace than before because of a combination of affordability pressures linked to higher inflation, higher borrowing costs, enhanced supply and the uncertain economic outlook.

Further interest rate hikes and no resolution to the Iran crisis are likely to accelerate this trend.

Daft’s snapshot of the market in the third quarter put headline annualised inflation (for asking prices) at 3 per cent, half the level that it was a year ago. In Dublin the rate of price growth was estimated at 2.7 per cent.

MyHome’s equivalent report, published on Tuesday this week, put asking price inflation at 3.9 per cent and at 2.1 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s official numbers, also published on Tuesday, put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent in August and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago, so there’s a lag. Because they are based on asking prices, the MyHome and Daft reports provide more of an instant snapshot of which way the market is turning.

The CSO estimates the average price paid for a property nationally in the 12 months to August was €442,512, while in Dublin it was €598,677.

For MyHome, the average price nationally was €461,084 and €585,132 in Dublin. For Daft, the figures were €445,000 and €635,000.

The CSO and MyHome use median (middle value) prices in their reports instead of average prices.

With any property price survey, there is a need to distinguish between quality-adjusted price changes [those controlled for location, property type, new versus old homes, etc] and pure price inflation.

The CSO breaks its figures down by Eircode, which reveals significant price disparities not just between Dublin and the rest of the State but also within the capital itself.

Take, for example, the difference between Dublin 6, which covers Ranelagh and Rathgar, where the average price paid for properties last year was just shy of €1 million (€995,709), making it the most expensive Eircode in the State, and Dublin 10, which includes Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard, where the average price was €333,391.

Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite

According to MyHome, house prices in Tuam in Galway have risen by 10.2 per cent in 2026 while prices in Kilkee in Clare have slumped by almost 13 per cent.

So while the CSO, MyHome and Daft capture the general direction of travel, they can differ significantly because of the disparity between asking prices and actual sale prices.

Put another way, MyHome and Daft measure what sellers want; the CSO measures what buyers actually pay.

Moynihan – who speaks quietly and sometimes mumbles – was a surprise choice to lead the group in late 2009. The board was known to have been searching for an outside star after Lewis resigned amid a shareholder backlash following the disastrous Merrill deal.

EU hub post Brexit

Bank of America chose Dublin as its EU headquarters in 2017 in the wake of the Brexit referendum. The unit has two main divisions: global banking and markets, and support services, which includes a global technology and operations centre.

The US banking giant has had a presence in the Republic since 1968. It has more than 1,000 employees in Dublin and about 400 contractors.

The group opened a new office in Belfast late last year and announced last week that it had hired more than 300 staff there, initially focused on anti-money laundering and financial crime compliance. It has a goal of creating up to 1,000 roles in the North.

“We knew the talent was there. We knew that there was capacity, with office space and other things we could get. And it’s a city that’s continuing to grow,” Moynihan said. “We knew we were going to have to expand this business, because it always grows when the business grows.”

All told, Bank of America has about 210,000 employees across 35 countries – broadly the same headcount as in 2007, even though it took on about 76,000 staff through its 2008 acquisitions of Merrill Lynch and mortgage lender Countrywide Financial.

Moynihan has said that Bank of America’s ongoing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is focused on getting more out of its workforce rather than cutting jobs. The bank has rolled out around 150 AI use cases across the group so far, with “hundreds” more in the pipeline, he said.

He said there is little room for error when rolling out AI to customers, because trust, security and reliability are fundamental to a banking relationship.

“If we used it to make loans, and it turned somebody down, and they alleged we turned them down because of whatever non-valid credit-based decision ... and the [AI agent] couldn’t explain its work, that’s where the agents are going to be tricky to implement.”

Moynihan declined to be dragged into the AI bubble debate, deferring to research last week from the bank’s market strategists, who noted that a narrow group of AI companies has been driving the Nasdaq 100 Index to all-time highs recently. “Low breadth is a classic feature of bubbles building and typically doesn’t stop until they pop,” they said.

Bank of America’s shares surged more than fourfold between Moynihan taking charge in 2010 and mid-August. Its annual profits grew at a similar pace even as total assets rose by only 60 per cent. The $1.2 billion fine – while embarrassing – equates to about 3.6 per cent of the group’s net income for the 12 months to the end of September, and has only brought the stock back to where it was in late May.

The CEO lives in Wellesley, Massachusetts, an affluent suburb west of Boston, and divides his working time between Boston and the group’s headquarters in Charlotte.

Succession planning moved up a notch 13 months ago when the bank promoted two executives – Dean Athanasia and Jim DeMare – to co-presidents of the entire business, and chief financial officer Alastair Borthwick was given the title of executive vice-president.

But Moynihan was coy when asked how long he planned to stick around.

“I don’t talk about it,” he said. “But I expect to serve as long as the board will have me and I’m having fun.”

Job: CEO of Bank of America.

Age: 67.

Family: Married to Susan Berry, whom he met at college, with three adult children.

Lives: Wellesley, near Boston in Massachusetts.

For years, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) has advised successive ministers for finance to go easy on the spending increases and tax cuts, put away more money and account properly for the possibility of overruns.

Yet, time and again on budget day, much of the advice appears to be quietly ignored.

Take Budget 2027, for example.

The budgetary process now begins several months before the big day itself – with the Stability Programme Update in April, followed by the Summer Economic Statement (SES) in July. Between them, the two documents provide a good sense of what will be at the Government’s disposal later in the year.

Ifac’s position was that if the Government continued down this road, then its policies would only add to an already worrying inflation outlook.

While winning plaudits from external reviewers, some politicians have eyed Ifac with a little suspicion over the years.

At a time when Ireland was crying out for public investment, particularly in housing, it has been accused of sometimes offering a narrow and needlessly cautious prescription. Yes, the argument went, the economy is doing well, but there are huge gaps where more money should also be spent.

How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?

Sinn Féin’s spokesman on finance, Pearse Doherty, says there could be “question marks” over some of Ifac’s warnings down through the years, which were perhaps “too conservative”.

“If we look back at Ifac’s recommendations – and they have gone unheeded by the government in the past – the economy has still continued to grow and continued to have surpluses,” he says.

However, he says the council has played an important role over recent budgets in highlighting consistent spending overruns.

The groupthink that prevailed in the pre-crisis period, so the argument goes, is no longer a problem.

With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis?

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[Revenue looks to reduce postal costs and transition to ‘digital-first’ communications]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/revenue-looks-to-reduce-postal-costs-and-transition-to-digital-first-communications/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/revenue-looks-to-reduce-postal-costs-and-transition-to-digital-first-communications/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Revenue is looking at ways to reduce postal communications with taxpayers and expand the use of “robotics” and artificial intelligence (AI) to deal with queries.

The tax authority is reviewing its postage practices, which cost it around €14.8 million in 2025, and increase the use of its online platform to send out important tax documents to millions of taxpayers each year.

In budget documents published alongside Budget 2027 last week it was stated that Revenue was “developing new systems and processes to transition” some customers to “digital-only” communication methods.

However, a spokeswoman for Revenue told The Irish Times that its work “is focused on transitioning towards a digital-first approach, rather than digital-only communications”.

This means “prioritising digital correspondence where appropriate, while continuing to provide postal communications where necessary”, she added.

Taxpayers who are registered for an account with Revenue’s online service but still receive correspondence by post will be the initial focus of the review.

Some 4.6 million people are registered for the MyAccount platform, according to figures from Revenue.

Tax credit certificates (TCCs) and statements of liability have been “identified as particular areas of focus”, the spokeswoman said. Revenue sent out 1.4 million TCCs in 2025 and more than 600,000 statements of liability, at a total cost of around €3.7 million.

In total, Revenue issued almost 10 million postal items in 2025, equivalent to a little more than 3.4 per cent of the total number of letters delivered by An Post in the same year, according to its annual report.

OPW paid large Revenue settlement over renting properties to staff at below market rates

Asked about the impact of Revenue’s move towards digital communications, a spokeswoman for An Post said the shift has “been the reality” for more than a decade across Government.

“The commitment to e-government and digitalisation of communications ... has been part of government policy over several administrations,” she said.

“This has fuelled An Post’s transformation to become a major ecommerce parcel and logistics company, digitalising our own processes across the business.”

She said An Post was also reviewing its strategic priorities to decide where to focus future investment. “We are hugely ambitious about taking opportunities to further expand and modernise the business in a digital world,” she said.

Revenue received a budget allocation of €684 million for next year, up around 4 per cent, according to the Budget 2027 expenditure report.

Apart from the review of its postal practices, other “efficiencies” and reforms that the tax authority is expected to deliver include an expansion of its “AI and robotics portfolio of applications into customer service channels”.

New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months

For several years, Revenue has been using robotics to speed up mundane internal processes and free up staff to do other tasks.

The Irish Times reported in 2019 that Revenue had teamed up with Deloitte for a pilot project using robotic process automation technology to update some 20,000 taxpayer records.

Earlier this year, Revenue commissioner Ruth Kennedy told the Oireachtas AI committee that the authority did not use AI to make “tax-related decisions or carry out its statutory functions”. However, she said Revenue had been using the technology for a long time “to assist in more accurately directing taxpayer queries” to caseworkers, and assisting staff in finding “relevant information” to respond to taxpayer queries, “promptly and accurately”.

]]>Marek SLUSARCZYK<![CDATA[Plan for O’Connell Street restaurant approved, but it is banned from serving takeaways]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/plan-for-oconnell-street-restaurant-approved-but-it-is-banned-from-serving-takeaways/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/plan-for-oconnell-street-restaurant-approved-but-it-is-banned-from-serving-takeaways/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000A new restaurant being planned for Ulster Bank’s former O’Connell Street branch in Dublin will be barred from operating any takeaway food service.

Kingstonway Limited, the new owners of 2-4 O’Connell Street Lower, applied for planning permission to convert the building into a mixed-use restaurant, retail and office development.

Dublin City Council has now granted the company permission to convert part of the old bank into a restaurant, but said it “shall not operate as a takeaway (an outlet that sells hot food for consumption off the premises)”.

In its planning application, the company said it had interest from an international restaurant operator to occupy part of the building, but did not clarify if this operator wanted to provide takeaway services.

Longstanding concerns have been aired by city councillors about the concentration of fast-food outlets on O’Connell Street, from which about a dozen provide takeaway services.

The pushback on new takeaway food businesses on O’Connell Street by the council has come as US takeaway brands, including Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken, Wendy’s and Taco Bell, are expanding into the Irish market.

In 2024, a Dublin City Taskforce led by former An Post chief executive David McRedmond said the Government needed to “revitalise O’Connell Street and environs” through the use of the Special Planning Control Scheme (SPCS).

There are two SPCS in place at present in central Dublin, which cover Grafton Street, O’Connell Street and their surrounding areas.

The SPCS set out a number of policies and objectives on architectural conservation, property uses, building heights, advertising signs and shopfronts, vacancy and civic identity.

In its decision to approve the new O’Connell Street restaurant, the city council cited the SPCS for the area as its reason for banning takeaway services from the venue.

The project to revamp the old Ulster Bank branch is being led by the building’s owners, Kingstonway Limited. The company is linked to eShopWorld founder Tommy Kelly and former BidX1 chief executive Stephen McCarthy.

Kelly, whose wealth has been estimated to be about €1 billion, made a large amount of his fortune from the €600 million sale of ecommerce company eShopWorld.

Following the sale in 2021, he has made a number of investments in property and businesses through CastleGate Investments, including a deal to acquire estate agent Sherry Fitzgerald.

Kelly and McCarthy’s plans for 2-4 O’Connell Street Lower have come a year after the building was put up for sale by Ulster Bank at a guide price of €2.75 million.

The restaurant planned would take up 734sq m across the basement, ground and mezzanine levels of the refurbished building, with 941sq m of office space on the upper floors.

The plans for the building align with a recommendation from the Dublin City Taskforce, which called for more mixed-use buildings on O’Connell Street, including residential, hospitality, cultural and night-time use alongside the existing retail and commercial usage.

A multiyear programme, in partnership with private landlords, to revitalise O’Connell Street and adjoining streets was also required to foster “development of the area as a cultural hub”, the taskforce said.

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[To get into Ireland’s top 1%, you’ll need €123,000 in disposable income]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/to-get-into-irelands-top-1-youll-need-123000-in-disposable-income/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/to-get-into-irelands-top-1-youll-need-123000-in-disposable-income/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000To rank among Ireland’s top 1 per cent of earners, an individual needs to generate €123,200 of disposable income a year, a new study has revealed.

The threshold or entry point to the elite earners category in Ireland is the third highest in the EU, research by Berlin-based DataPulse found.

Only Luxembourg at €205,420 and Denmark at €135,389 had higher thresholds. Ireland’s entry point is higher than that of Germany (€111,693), the Netherlands (€107,894) and France (€104,743).

The findings, which used Eurostat data on disposable income across member states, are part of a wider “European income ladder” study commissioned by lifestyle and travel magazine AMEXcited.

It found that Ireland also has the third-highest share of its own population among the EU’s top 1 per cent of earners.

Some 2.48 per cent of the Irish population, equating to 134,900 individuals, belong to the EU-wide top 1 per cent category, which has a threshold of €92,200 of annual disposable income per person after taxes and social contributions.

Germany and France together account for about 59 per cent of the EU-wide top 1 per cent by income, with roughly 35 per cent in Germany and 24 per cent in France.

The report also measured “the gap between the middle and the top”. In Ireland, the top 1 per cent earning threshold, €123,200, was 3½ times the median disposable income of €35,138.

This compares to 5½ times in Bulgaria – the highest – and just 2.4 times in Slovakia – the lowest.

Household wealth in Ireland hits record €1.4tn

The survey also measured how much EU heads of government and members of national parliaments earn compared to people on median gross incomes in those member states.

In Ireland, Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s gross salary – €256,311 a year – was five times that of the gross median income at €51,781.

TDs, who get paid €119,467 a year, earned 2.3 times the gross median income.

The German chancellor earns €333,704 a year, 6.3 times the German median income at €53,098.

Chief executives in EU markets were found to earn between 100 and 700 times median salaries in their respective countries.

The best-paid chief executive in Ireland in 2024, according to the report, was Kerry Group chief executive Edmond Scanlon on €6 million, which was 117 times median earnings here.

CEO pay in Ireland in 2025: One executive earned $237m

Separate studies suggest former Flutter chief executive Peter Jackson, who stepped down this year, had a bigger salary than Scanlon.

At the very top of the DataPulse chart was Lucian Grainge of Universal Music Group in the Netherlands, on €41.1 million a year, which was 690 times the national median earnings.

“The best-paid Dutch CEO earns in one year what 690 years of median work would pay,” the report said.

The study only considered regular pay components for a single financial year – base salary, annual bonus, pension and benefits – and not severance or one-off special awards.

When working time instead of salaries is considered, the gap between company chiefs and average workers looks even starker.

Grainge reaches the median Dutch gross monthly earnings in about 11 minutes of work, while the chief executive of the German software giant SAP, Christian Klein, reaches the German median income in about 25 minutes.

A German full-time employee on the minimum wage, by contrast, would need about 576 years to reach the SAP chief executive’s pay.

]]>miniseries<![CDATA[Johnny Sexton to advise Johnstown Collection on ‘culture’ during €40m investment]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/johnny-sexton-to-advise-johnstown-collection-on-culture-during-40m-investment/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/johnny-sexton-to-advise-johnstown-collection-on-culture-during-40m-investment/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Johnny Sexton has been appointed as an adviser to the Johnstown Collection, the luxury hotel chain behind the Johnstown and Mount Juliet estates, as the group undergoes an investment of almost €40 million across its portfolio.

The former Ireland rugby captain’s role is to advise the group’s senior leadership team with a “focus on team behaviours, culture, accountability and continuous improvement” in order to improve its standing among international organisations and corporate clients, the company said in a statement.

“I’m looking forward to sharing my perspective and my own experiences with the team in all these areas, building on what is already there and, together, achieving new levels of success,” Sexton said. “Not just in Ireland, but on an international level, too.”

He will also work to evolve the sporting and training facilities on offer at the Johnstown Estate in Co Meath through providing an “external perspective and high-performance insight” to operations and management, the company said.

The hotel group, which is owned by Winthrop Technologies founder Barry English, said it was experiencing “significant investment and growth” across its portfolio, with “over €39.5 million invested and planned” to be spent.

Some €26 million of this is earmarked for Johnstown Estate, while €8 million and €5.5 million are designated for Mount Juliet Estate in Co Kilkenny and Trim Castle Hotel in Co Meath, respectively.

The Irish Times understands the investment is primarily to increase capacity and expand facilities across the group’s properties.

Proposed developments include a rooftop thermal suite at Trim Castle Hotel and an additional 90 bedrooms and a new restaurant at Johnstown Estate, designed to expand revenues across the collection’s leisure and corporate markets.

Johnny Sexton joins private equity firm Exponent

Sean Reid, the Johnstown Collection’s commercial director, said Sexton’s appointment “is about aligning our business with the standards and mindset that define elite performance”.

“In hospitality, the difference is often in the small details, and Johnny’s experience will help us sharpen our focus as we continue to strengthen our offering even further for corporate clients and high-performing organisations,” Reid said.

The group’s general manager, Anthony Smiddy, said: “Johnny brings a unique perspective and wealth of experience that will help us realise the ambition we have for the Johnstown Collection over the coming years.”

]]><![CDATA[More than half of under-12s have overnight access to smart devices, survey says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/social-affairs/2026/10/16/more-than-half-of-under-12s-have-overnight-access-to-smart-devices-survey-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/social-affairs/2026/10/16/more-than-half-of-under-12s-have-overnight-access-to-smart-devices-survey-says/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000More than half of children under 12 have access to smartphones and other internet-connected devices in their bedrooms overnight, a survey has found, with a third saying they faced no restrictions on their online activity.

That rose to about two-thirds for children aged between 12 and 15, the report from online safety charity CyberSafeKids said.

However, parents were also guilty of failing to put their smartphones down, with more than half of young people saying parents were on their devices all or most of the time they were with their children.

“The research highlights the near-constant connectivity of even very young children. Screens in bedrooms, especially overnight, affect not only sleep but overall wellbeing,” CyberSafeKids chief executive Alex Cooney said.

“Children need clear boundaries around device use at home, and the fact that many have no restrictions at all is alarming, given the harmful content and contact inherent in digital environments.”

Most children under 15 reported going online in the evening, with a fifth of eight to 12-year-olds and 37 per cent of under-15s saying they fell asleep with devices.

Almost a quarter of teens were going online as soon as they woke up, and 41 per cent of 12 to 15-year-olds were accessing the internet before school.

The survey, which questioned 1,200 children, also found that young people were finding it more difficult to switch off from products designed to keep them online.

The results were published in advance of CyberBreak 2026, a HSE-supported initiative to encourage families, schools and workplaces to switch off smart devices for 24 hours from 7pm on Friday, avoiding social media, online apps, gaming and non-essential messaging.

More than 25,000 people have already committed to the initiative, which is promoting healthier digital habits.

Psychotherapist Richard Hogan said parents must lead by example.

“This means engaging with our kids before our phones in the morning and during the day – sending the vital message to them that they come first, not our smart devices,” he said.

“It’s our responsibility to help them switch off, unplug and reconnect with what matters most.”

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444830/">
   <title>Neuer Balkan-Pop inmitten alter Konflikte</title>
   <description>Der Westbalkan hat einen neuen Popstar: Der 21-jährige Kroate Jakov Jozinovic füllt Hallen in der Region und trat am Samstag erstmals nahe Wien auf. Bekannt wurde er mit Neuinterpretationen beliebter Balkan-Klassiker. Doch ein Video, das ihn beim Singen eines Liedes des rechtsextremen kroatischen Musikers Thompson zeigt, löste Mitte Oktober heftige Proteste aus. Jozinovic erklärte, er habe „niemanden verletzen wollen“, der Vorfall entfacht erneut Debatten über nationale Identität und die Aufarbeitung der Vergangenheit auf dem Balkan.</description>

Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.

Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.
